lead: Single-sideband (SSB) and vestigial-sideband (VSB) modulation are bandwidth-saving children of double-sideband suppressed-carrier (DSB-SC) modulation. DSB-SC sends two sidebands, but each sideband carries the same message information. SSB transmits only one sideband, so bandwidth falls from 2W to W. VSB transmits one full sideband plus a narrow vestige of the other, so a real filter can build it. Radio links, point-to-point voice, and analog TV video use these ideas.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.2 DSB-SC modulation and coherent detection and Unit 1 Hilbert transform and complex envelope.

blocks.text: Let the message m(t) have bandwidth W hertz and let the carrier be cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t, where f<sub>c</sub> is the carrier frequency in hertz. DSB-SC forms s(t) = m(t) cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t. Its spectrum has an upper sideband from f<sub>c</sub> to f<sub>c</sub> + W and a lower sideband from f<sub>c</sub> − W to f<sub>c</sub>. For a real message these two sidebands are mirror images. Each one contains the full message spectrum, so one can be removed and the receiver can still recover m(t).

SSB sends only one sideband. Its bandwidth is B<sub>SSB</sub> = W. The upper-sideband signal occupies f<sub>c</sub> to f<sub>c</sub> + W; the lower-sideband signal occupies f<sub>c</sub> − W to f<sub>c</sub>. A 3 kHz audio band therefore needs 3 kHz of radio spectrum in SSB, against 6 kHz in DSB-SC. The price is a sharper filter or a more careful modulator, and a coherent receiver with a well synchronized local carrier.
B<sub>DSB</sub> = 2W, B<sub>SSB</sub> = W, B<sub>VSB</sub> = W + f<sub>v</sub>
blocks.where: W is message bandwidth in Hz; f<sub>v</sub> is vestige width in Hz; B is occupied RF bandwidth in Hz.

blocks.text: Coherent detection multiplies the received SSB signal by 2 cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t and low-pass filters with cutoff W. A phase error φ in the local carrier attenuates the message by cos φ and adds Hilbert-transform crosstalk; a frequency error makes the output beat and sound distorted. Some syllabi call SSB single-sideband suppressed carrier, or SSB-SC.

The filter method starts from a DSB-SC signal. A band-pass filter keeps one sideband and rejects the other. The two sidebands meet at f<sub>c</sub>, so the filter must change from stop to pass within the width of the message. For 3 kHz audio at a high carrier frequency this is a very sharp filter, and every decibel of opposite-sideband leakage becomes interference.

The phase-shift method cancels one sideband by adding two DSB-SC terms in quadrature. One branch multiplies m(t) by cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t. The other multiplies m̂(t) by sin 2πf<sub>c</sub>t, where m̂(t) is the Hilbert transform of m(t): every frequency component is shifted by 90°, as in Unit 1. Adding or subtracting cancels the unwanted sideband.

s<sub>USB</sub>(t) = (A<sub>c</sub>/2)[m(t) cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t − m̂(t) sin 2πf<sub>c</sub>t]
s<sub>LSB</sub>(t) = (A<sub>c</sub>/2)[m(t) cos 2πf<sub>c</sub>t + m̂(t) sin 2πf<sub>c</sub>t]
blocks.where: A<sub>c</sub> is the carrier amplitude in volts; m(t) is the message; m̂(t) is its Hilbert transform; f<sub>c</sub> is the carrier frequency in Hz; USB is upper sideband and LSB is lower sideband.

blocks.text: Practical cancellation needs the two branches to match in amplitude and phase. A small mismatch leaves a residual sideband. The Weaver method uses two stages of quadrature modulation and low-pass filtering. It avoids both a sharp RF filter and a wideband 90° phase shifter, at the cost of more mixers and filters.
SSB is used in point-to-point HF radio, in some telephone multiplexing, and in any link where spectrum is scarce. It is not a good fit for a simple envelope detector because it has no carrier.

sections.h3: VSB: one full sideband and a vestige

blocks.text: VSB (vestigial sideband) keeps one sideband in full and a narrow vestige of the other sideband near the carrier. Let f<sub>v</sub> be the vestige width in hertz. Then B<sub>VSB</sub> = W + f<sub>v</sub>. The vestige is small, so VSB bandwidth sits between SSB and DSB. A 3 kHz message with a 0.5 kHz vestige occupies 3.5 kHz, not 6 kHz.

The reason is practical filtering. A real band-pass filter has a gradual transition from passband to stopband. VSB uses that transition as the vestige instead of demanding an almost ideal edge at f<sub>c</sub>. The receiver can equalize the vestige, or, in television, use a large transmitted carrier and an envelope detector. Analog TV video is the standard example: it sends one video sideband fully and a small vestige of the other, with the carrier present.

VSB is not SSB with an accidentally wide filter. The vestige is a defined part of the spectrum and must be accounted for in bandwidth and detection. It is also not DSB: the far sideband is rejected. The occupied band is W + f<sub>v</sub>, so a 0.5 kHz vestige adds 0.5 kHz to the SSB bandwidth, not 3 kHz.

figure.caption: The product modulator shifts the 0-3 kHz audio band to a 100 kHz carrier. The filter keeps the full upper sideband and a 0.5 kHz vestige of the lower sideband, so the VSB output occupies 3.5 kHz.

spec.title: SSB or VSB by filtering
spec.aria: A 0-3 kHz audio band and a 100 kHz carrier enter a product modulator; a band-pass filter keeps the upper sideband and a 0.5 kHz vestige to produce SSB or VSB.

examples.question: A 0-3 kHz audio band modulates a 100 kHz carrier. Compare the DSB, SSB and VSB bandwidths if the VSB filter keeps a 0.5 kHz vestige. Give the occupied RF range for the SSB upper sideband and for the VSB signal.
steps: Message bandwidth W = 3 kHz, carrier f<sub>c</sub> = 100 kHz, vestige width f<sub>v</sub> = 0.5 kHz.
DSB bandwidth B<sub>DSB</sub> = 2W = 2 × 3 = 6 kHz. It occupies 100 − 3 = 97 kHz to 100 + 3 = 103 kHz.
SSB bandwidth B<sub>SSB</sub> = W = 3 kHz. The upper sideband occupies f<sub>c</sub> to f<sub>c</sub> + W = 100 kHz to 103 kHz.
VSB bandwidth B<sub>VSB</sub> = W + f<sub>v</sub> = 3 + 0.5 = 3.5 kHz. The filter keeps the full upper sideband 100-103 kHz and a 0.5 kHz lower-sideband vestige 99.5-100 kHz.
The VSB occupied range is therefore 99.5 kHz to 103 kHz. Against DSB, SSB saves 3 kHz (50%) and VSB saves 2.5 kHz (about 41.7%).
examples.answer: DSB needs 6 kHz, SSB needs 3 kHz, and VSB needs 3.5 kHz; the SSB upper sideband occupies 100-103 kHz and the VSB signal occupies about 99.5-103 kHz.
examples.check:
W = 3.0  # kHz
fv = 0.5  # kHz
dsb = 2 * W
ssb = W
vsb = W + fv
print(dsb)
print(ssb)
print(vsb)

traps: SSB is not one fixed spectrum: say upper sideband or lower sideband. 'SSB' alone does not tell the examiner which half of the DSB spectrum remains.
The filter method is judged by opposite-sideband rejection in decibels. A finite filter always leaks some of the unwanted sideband; ideal brick-wall filters do not exist.
VSB bandwidth is W + f<sub>v</sub>, not W and not 2W. The vestige width f<sub>v</sub> is measured near the carrier, not the full message bandwidth.
Coherent SSB detection needs carrier synchronization. A phase error is not just a gain error: it adds crosstalk; a frequency error causes a beat.
VSB is not SSB with a sloppy filter. The vestige is deliberate and is included in the bandwidth and receiver design.

quiz.q: What is the RF bandwidth of an SSB signal whose message bandwidth is W?
quiz.a: B = W, because only one sideband is transmitted.

quiz.q: Why can one sideband be removed in SSB without losing the message?
quiz.a: For a real message the two sidebands are mirror images around the carrier and carry the same spectral content. A coherent detector uses the remaining sideband to recover the message.

quiz.q: A 0-4 kHz message is transmitted as SSB on a 50 kHz carrier. State the occupied band for USB and for LSB, and the bandwidth.
quiz.a: USB: 50-54 kHz. LSB: 46-50 kHz. B = W = 4 kHz.

quiz.q: A VSB signal has W = 5 kHz and f<sub>v</sub> = 0.8 kHz. Compare its bandwidth with DSB and SSB, and give one practical reason for VSB.
quiz.a: VSB B = 5.8 kHz; DSB = 10 kHz; SSB = 5 kHz. VSB saves 4.2 kHz over DSB but uses 0.8 kHz more than SSB; the vestige lets a real filter have a gradual edge.

quiz.q: Name the three SSB generation methods.
quiz.a: Filter method, phase-shift method, Weaver method.

quiz.q: Why does the phase-shift SSB method need a Hilbert transform?
quiz.a: It needs a 90° shifted copy m̂(t) so the two quadrature branches can cancel one sideband; the Hilbert transform gives that π/2 shift to every frequency component.

quiz.q: In a coherent SSB detector the local carrier has a small phase error φ. What happens to the output? What if the local frequency is off by Δf?
quiz.a: The wanted message is attenuated by cos φ and a Hilbert-transform crosstalk term appears. A frequency error Δf makes the output beat at Δf and distorts the recovered speech.

beyond: Not for the exam. SSB remains important in HF radio, military links, and spectrum-crowded satellite and utility networks. Practical SSB transmitters use crystal or ceramic filters, digital Hilbert filters, or Weaver-style DSP modulators. VSB appears in analog TV and in the ATSC 8-VSB digital television standard used in some countries. Search next for Hilbert transform filters, Weaver modulator, and 8-VSB.
